title: She Is Seventeen. She Beat the Fifth Seed. At the Australian Open, Indian Women Owned the Draw.
excerpt: PV Sindhu cruised into the quarterfinals, Tanvi Sharma produced the upset of the tournament, and four Indian women advanced — while every Indian man was eliminated in Sydney.
body:
Four Indian women advanced past the opening round. Every Indian man was eliminated before the draw thinned. At the Australian Open Super 500 in Sydney, the state of Indian badminton split cleanly along gender lines — and the women's side of the ledger has never looked more promising.

## Sindhu Was Efficient. Tanvi Was Electric.

PV Sindhu, seeded third, dealt with her first-round opponent in the manner of someone who had somewhere else to be. The two-time Olympic medallist dispatched Peru's Ines Lucia Castillo 21-13, 21-11 in 32 minutes, never once allowing the match to feel like a contest.

In the round of 16, she faced a trickier proposition — fellow Indian Isharani Baruah, who had earned her place with a gutsy three-game victory over China's Han Qian Xi (22-20, 10-21, 21-14) in the previous round. But Sindhu was too precise, winning 22-20, 21-12 to book a quarterfinal berth where she will face Chinese Taipei's Chen Shu-yu.

The former world champion has been chasing her first BWF World Tour title since winning the Syed Modi International in 2024. Sydney, with its favourable draw and her current form, represents her strongest chance in months.

But the standout result belonged to someone two decades her junior.

Tanvi Sharma is 17 years old. She was not expected to trouble the fifth seed, Chiu Pin-chian of Chinese Taipei, ranked 11th in the world. She did more than trouble her. The teenager won 21-12, 22-20 — the first set a demolition, the second a display of composure that belied her age.

It was the kind of upset that reshapes how a player is perceived overnight. Before Sydney, Tanvi was a name on a junior circuit. After it, she is a name in a major Super 500 draw, set to face fellow Indian Malvika Bansod in the next round.

## The Depth Behind the Headlines

Bansod's own journey to the round of 16 was not straightforward. She lost the first game to Thailand's Tonrug Saeheng 15-21 before reasserting herself emphatically — 21-7, 21-13 in the final two games. The comeback was a reminder that Bansod, at her best, possesses one of the sharpest attacking games in the women's circuit.

Tanya Hemanth rounded out the Indian women's advance with a steady straight-games win over USA's Ishika Jaiswal, 21-17, 21-18.

Four Indian women in the round of 16 at a Super 500 event. It is not unprecedented, but it is rare, and it speaks to a depth that Indian women's badminton has been building quietly over the past few years.

## The Men's Side Told a Different Story

There is no polite way to say it: India's men had a miserable opening day. Kiran George, Tharun Mannepalli, and qualifier Saneeth Dayanand were all eliminated in the first round. Not one Indian male shuttler survived to see the second day of competition.

The absences told part of the story. Lakshya Sen, the reigning Australian Open champion, was not in the draw. Kidambi Srikanth sat out as well. The doubles pair of Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty, who could have competed in men's doubles, withdrew with injuries.

But absences only explain so much. The men who were present lost comprehensively, without the close-fought defeats that might signal progress.

## What It Means for the NRI Fan

For diaspora fans who have watched Indian badminton's trajectory since Sindhu's historic Olympic silver in Rio, the women's dominance in Sydney affirms a deeper trend. India's female shuttlers are no longer reliant on one or two stars. Behind Sindhu, there is now a bench — Tanvi, Malvika, Tanya, Isharani, Aakarshi Kashyap — any of whom can win matches at the highest level.

The quarterfinals begin Thursday, June 12. Sindhu faces Chen Shu-yu. A Tanvi-Bansod clash would guarantee another Indian in the semifinal. For a sport that still fights for screen time against cricket, the women are making a quiet, unanswerable case for attention.
